title: Availability Patterns
description: Explore common patterns for achieving high availability in distributed systems.

data.text: High availability means a system remains operational and reachable despite component failures. In practice, availability targets are expressed in nines: 99.9% allows about 8.7 hours of downtime per year, while 99.999% allows only five minutes. Reaching high availability requires removing single points of failure, automating recovery, and ensuring traffic can be redirected around failed nodes with minimal human intervention.

data.title: Patterns That Improve Availability
items: Redundancy: deploy multiple instances across zones so one failure does not take down the service.
Health checks: detect unhealthy instances and remove them from service automatically.
Failover: route traffic from a failed primary to a standby secondary.
Load balancing: spread traffic across healthy instances to prevent overload.
Graceful degradation: disable non-essential features during load to preserve core functionality.
Circuit breaker: stop sending traffic to a failing dependency and return fallbacks.

data.caption: Availability patterns form a layered defense against failures.
data.definition:
flowchart TD

    LB -->|health check| HC{Healthy?}
    HC -->|Yes| Inst[Instance Pool]
    HC -->|No| Fallback[Fallback Response]
    Inst -->|primary fails| Failover[Failover Controller]
    Failover --> Standby[Standby Instance]
    Inst -.->|circuit open| CB[Circuit Breaker]
    CB -.->|return cache| Cache[Cache / Fallback]

data.title: No Silver Bullet
data.text: Availability patterns work together but also add complexity. More replicas mean more failure modes, and failover logic can itself fail. Always test your recovery mechanisms, not just your happy path.

Active-passive systems run one primary and one or more standby replicas. The standby takes over only when the primary fails. This is simple but wastes resources during normal operation. Active-active systems route traffic to multiple primitives simultaneously, improving utilization and reducing failover time. However, active-active requires conflict resolution because writes can arrive at different primaries out of order.

cards.title: Active-Passive
cards.description: One primary handles all writes; standby is idle until failover.
pros: No write conflicts during normal operation

cards.title: Active-Active
cards.description: Multiple primaries accept writes and serve reads simultaneously.

items.question: What is the difference between availability and uptime?
items.answer: Uptime measures whether a system is running. Availability measures whether it is reachable and responsive to valid requests. A system can be up but unavailable if the network path is broken.

items.question: Can I achieve five nines without active-active?
items.answer: It is difficult but possible with fast automated failover and multi-zone redundancy. Active-active simply makes the target more achievable.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Availability is a system property, not an instance property.
Redundancy removes single points of failure.
Health checks and load balancers automate traffic management.
Active-active improves utilization but requires conflict resolution.
Always test failover; assumptions about recovery are often wrong.
data.takeaway: High availability is built from layered patterns, not a single feature.
